transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. I... well, honestly, what brings me in is that I am just so incredibly exhausted. And I don't mean the normal kind of tired where you just need a good night's rest. It's like I'm exhausted in a way that sleep just doesn't fix at all. 

You know, usually, if I have a long week at the office—I'm a manager, so I'm used to handling a lot of moving parts and putting out fires all day—I can just sleep in on the weekend and bounce back. But lately, I go to bed early, I try to get a full eight or nine hours, and I wake up feeling just as drained as when I went to sleep. It's really frustrating because just getting through a normal workday right now feels... I don't know, it just feels so much heavier than it should. Like I'm dragging myself through molasses just to answer my emails or sit through a basic status meeting. 

And then by the time I get home, even something as simple as figuring out dinner and sitting down to eat feels like this insurmountable mountain. I used to be able to just transition from work mode to home mode without a second thought, but now it's just... it's all too much. I just don't understand why I have absolutely zero energy when I'm technically getting enough sleep, you know? It's just this heavy, heavy weight that won't lift, no matter what I do, and I just can't keep pushing through my days feeling like this.
Can you tell me if you've been feeling down or depressed most of the day, or if you've lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Well, yes, actually. I mean, it's not just the exhaustion, though that's a huge part of it, obviously. But it's also this... this mood that just settles over me. Most days lately, I wake up and there's just this heavy, gray feeling right from the moment I open my eyes. It's like I'm already disappointed in the day before it even starts, if that makes any sense. 

I'll just lie there for a minute, looking at the ceiling, and I just feel this immense lack of... anything good. It's not necessarily that I'm crying all the time, though I have had moments where I just feel like crying for no particular reason, like when I'm driving to work and a slightly sad song comes on the radio, or even just sitting at my desk staring at a spreadsheet. But mostly, it's just this pervasive, dull ache. 

And as for things I used to enjoy... well, I used to love gardening. My husband and I have this beautiful backyard, and I'd spend hours out there on the weekends, pruning the roses, weeding the vegetable patch. It was my way of decompressing from the stress of managing my team. But now? The weeds are taking over, and I look out the window at it, and I just... I don't care. I know I should care, I know it's a mess, but the thought of going out there and actually doing it just feels completely pointless. Even reading, which I usually do every night before bed—I've had the same novel sitting on my nightstand for three weeks, and I think I've read maybe two pages. It just all feels so flat and uninteresting. It's like the color has just been drained out of everything.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, not just occasionally or in response to specific stressors?

Yes, exactly. Like I was just trying to say, it really is almost every single day. It's not just a passing mood because I have a stressful quarterly review coming up at work or because someone on my team dropped the ball on a project. It's... well, it's just always there. 

Like I mentioned a moment ago, most days lately, I wake up and that heavy, gray feeling is already sitting right on top of me. I'll hear my alarm go off at 6:00 AM, and before my feet even touch the floor, before I even remember what day of the week it is or what I have scheduled, I'm just so incredibly disappointed that the day is even starting. It's like I'm defeated before I've even tried. 

And it just lingers, you know? It doesn't shake off. I'll go downstairs to make my coffee—I usually grind my own beans, this dark roast I usually love, and normally just the smell of it is enough to get me going in the morning—but lately I just stand there in the kitchen waiting for it to brew, and that gray cloud is just wrapped completely around me. I take it with me to the car, I take it into the office, it sits with me through all my meetings... So, yes, to answer your question, it's definitely not just occasionally or because of a specific problem I'm dealing with. It's just this constant, heavy backdrop to my entire day, from the very second I open my eyes.
Have you felt this way — down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day — for at least two weeks straight?

Well, I mean... it's hard to pinpoint exactly when it started, because it kind of just crept up on me, you know? Like, I didn't just wake up one Tuesday and think, "Aha, today is the day I feel terrible." It was more gradual. First, I just thought I was tired from the end-of-month reporting, and then maybe I thought I was coming down with something... but then, as I look back on it now, and I look at my calendar... I mean, we had my mother-in-law over for dinner on the 12th, and I remember feeling just completely hollow during that whole evening, barely able to follow the conversation. And that was... what, three weeks ago? 

So, yes, it's definitely been at least two weeks straight. Probably closer to three or four, honestly. Every single day, waking up with that same gray cloud, dragging myself through the motions, going to bed, and doing it all over again. It hasn't lifted for a single day in all that time. Not even on the weekends when I don't have to work. I just sit on the couch and stare at the wall, thinking about all the things I should be doing, like the gardening I mentioned, but I just... can't. It's just been this unbroken stretch of feeling completely weighed down and empty, day in and day out, for weeks now.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently, like eating much less than usual or losing weight without trying?

Well, now that you mention it... yes, I suppose I have. It's funny, my husband actually brought this up the other night. He usually makes dinner—he’s a fantastic cook, really, he makes this incredible roasted chicken with root vegetables that I normally just love—but lately, I just sit there and sort of push it around my plate. I’ll take a few bites, maybe eat a carrot or two, and then I just... I’m done. I don't even have the energy to chew, if that makes sense. It’s just picking at meals. 

And at work, it’s even worse. I used to be so good about taking a lunch break, even if it was just twenty minutes to go down to the cafeteria and grab a salad or a sandwich, just to get away from my desk. But lately, with everything feeling so heavy and me just staring at my computer screen trying to get through my emails, I’ll look up and it’s three in the afternoon and I completely forgot to eat lunch. I just forget. My assistant, Sarah, she even asked me yesterday if she should start bringing me a protein bar or something because she noticed I haven't been leaving my office at all. 

And because of all that, I guess, I have noticed my clothes are fitting differently. Like, my work skirts—the pencil skirts I usually wear to the office—they're definitely fitting a little looser around the waist. I actually had to safety-pin the waistband of my navy one on Tuesday just so it wouldn't twist around while I was in a meeting. And I'm certainly not trying to lose weight, believe me. I haven't been to the gym in weeks, obviously, with how exhausted I've been, so it's not from working out. It's just that the food... it just doesn't appeal to me at all anymore, and I just forget it even exists half the day.
Have you noticed that you're moving more slowly than usual, or that it's harder to get your body to do what you want it to do, like everything feels physically heavy or sluggish?

Well, yes, actually. It's... it's like wading through molasses, if that makes sense. And it's funny you ask about the physical heaviness because I was just talking about how exhausted I've been, but this feels different. It's not just the tiredness, it's like my actual brain and my mouth aren't connecting at the speed they used to. 

I really noticed it in our weekly staff meeting on Monday. Usually, I'm the one driving the agenda, right? I've got my notes, I'm firing off questions, I'm keeping everyone on track because, as a manager, if you don't keep the pace up, the whole hour just gets derailed by minor issues. But this past Monday... someone, I think it was David from accounting, asked me a pretty straightforward question about the Q3 projections. And I heard him, I understood the words, but there was this... this long, awkward pause. It was like I had to manually crank a gear in my head just to formulate the sentence, and then crank another gear to actually make my mouth say the words out loud. 

My assistant, Sarah—who I mentioned earlier, the one who asked about the protein bars—she actually pulled me aside afterward. She was very sweet about it, but she said, "Are you feeling okay? You just seemed a little... delayed today." And she's right. It’s like there’s this lag time now. A pause before I can get my thoughts and words moving. And it's not just in meetings, it's even when I'm just trying to type an email. My fingers just feel heavy on the keyboard, like every keystroke takes a conscious, deliberate effort instead of just flowing naturally like it used to. It's incredibly frustrating because I know what I want to say, I know what needs to be done, but my body and my brain are just dragging behind, like I'm wearing a lead suit.
Have you had any thoughts about hurting yourself or that life isn't worth living?

Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that. I mean, I know I've been talking about how incredibly heavy everything feels, and how I just sit on the couch staring at the wall, and the whole thing with the molasses and the lead suit... and I suppose when you put all of that together, it probably sounds very bleak, doesn't it? It sounds like someone who might just want to give up. But honestly, no. It's not like that at all. 

It's more of a... a profound frustration, I guess you could call it. I want to be doing things. I look out the window at my garden, and I see the weeds creeping into the flower beds, and I think, "I really need to get out there and pull those before they choke out the hydrangeas." I want to be the person who goes out and does that. I want to be the person who leads the staff meeting without that awful lag time. I want to be able to eat my husband's roasted chicken. 

So it's not that I don't want to be here, or that I think life isn't worth it. It's just that I feel trapped inside this version of myself that can't seem to execute any of the things I actually want to do. It's like being stuck in a waiting room, just waiting for this gray cloud to finally lift so I can get back to my actual life. I haven't had any thoughts about hurting myself, not for a second. I just want to feel like me again, you know? I just want the energy to participate in my own life.
Have you ever had a period like this before, where you felt down, exhausted, and lost interest in things, that lasted for weeks at a time?

Well, yes... yes, I have. It's funny, when you're in the middle of it, it feels like it's never going to end, and then when you're out of it, you almost convince yourself it wasn't that bad. But looking back, yes, there was a time. It was a few years ago, actually. I remember it so clearly because it started right around the holidays, which is usually my favorite time of year. I love hosting Thanksgiving, I usually do this huge spread, and then Christmas... but that year, I just couldn't. 

It started around November, and it just dragged on and on. I kept thinking, "Oh, it's just the winter blues, it's just the short days, it'll pass when spring comes." But it didn't. It just settled over me like this thick, heavy blanket. The longest stretch I can clearly remember—that specific time—it lasted about five months. Five whole months of just feeling so incredibly low and tired all the time. 

I was still going to work, still going through the motions, but it was just like I was describing earlier, everything was such a chore. I felt so unlike myself most days. My husband kept asking if I was coming down with something, like mono or a terrible flu that just wouldn't shake, because I would come home from work at 5:30 and just immediately put on my pajamas and get into bed. I didn't even want to watch TV or read, I just wanted to close my eyes. And that went on all the way through the spring. It wasn't until around April or maybe early May that I finally woke up one morning and felt like the fog had lifted a little bit, like I could finally take a full breath again. But yes, five months of just... slogging through every single day. It was awful.

doctor.question: Have you ever had a period like this before, where you felt down, exhausted, and lost interest in things, that lasted for weeks at a time?

patient.answer:
Well, yes... yes, I have. It's funny, when you're in the middle of it, it feels like it's never going to end, and then when you're out of it, you almost convince yourself it wasn't that bad. But looking back, yes, there was a time. It was a few years ago, actually. I remember it so clearly because it started right around the holidays, which is usually my favorite time of year. I love hosting Thanksgiving, I usually do this huge spread, and then Christmas... but that year, I just couldn't. 

It started around November, and it just dragged on and on. I kept thinking, "Oh, it's just the winter blues, it's just the short days, it'll pass when spring comes." But it didn't. It just settled over me like this thick, heavy blanket. The longest stretch I can clearly remember—that specific time—it lasted about five months. Five whole months of just feeling so incredibly low and tired all the time. 

I was still going to work, still going through the motions, but it was just like I was describing earlier, everything was such a chore. I felt so unlike myself most days. My husband kept asking if I was coming down with something, like mono or a terrible flu that just wouldn't shake, because I would come home from work at 5:30 and just immediately put on my pajamas and get into bed. I didn't even want to watch TV or read, I just wanted to close my eyes. And that went on all the way through the spring. It wasn't until around April or maybe early May that I finally woke up one morning and felt like the fog had lifted a little bit, like I could finally take a full breath again. But yes, five months of just... slogging through every single day. It was awful.
